title: Obedience to rulers, but no oath by the emperor’s fortune
source_text: Ἡμῖν μέντοι γε καταφρονητέον ἐξευμενισμοῦ ἀνθρώπων καὶ βασιλέων, οὐ μόνον ἐὰν διὰ μιαιφονιῶν καὶ ἀσελγειῶν καὶ ὠμοτάτων πράξεων ἐξευμενιζώμεθα αὐτοὺς, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐὰν διὰ τῆς εἰς τὸν θεὸν τῶν ὅλων ἀσεβείας ἤ τινος μετὰ δουλοπρεπείας καὶ ταπεινότητος φωνῆς, ἀλλοτρίας ἀνδρείων καὶ μεγαλοψύχων ἀνδρῶν καὶ τὴν καρτερίαν ὡς μεγίστην ἀρετὴν συναναλαβεῖν ταῖς ἄλλαις ἐθελόντων. ἔνθα μέντοι οὐδὲν ἐναντίον πράττομεν νόμῳ καὶ λόγῳ θεοῦ, οὐ μεμήναμεν οὐδ᾿ ὁρμῶμεν καθ᾿ ἑαυτῶν ἐγείρειν βασιλέως ἢ δυνάστου θυμὸν, ἐπὶ αἰκίας καὶ βασανιστήρια ἢ καὶ θανάτους ἡμᾶς φέροντα. ἀνέγνωμεν γὰρ καὶ τὸ „πᾶσα ψυχὴ ἐξουσίαις ὑπερεχούσαις ὑποτασσέσθω. οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ἐξουσία εἰ μὴ ὑπὸ θεοῦ, αἱ δὲ οὖσαι ὑπὸ θεοῦ τεταγμέναι εἰσίν· ὥστε οἱ ἀνθεστηκότες τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ τῇ τοῦ θεοῦ διαταγῇ ἀνθίστανται.“ ἐν μέντοι γε τοῖς εἰς τὴν πρὸς Ῥωμαίους ἐξηγητικοῖς, ὡς δυνατὸν ἦν ἡμῖν, ἐπὶ πλεῖον καὶ ταῦτα τὰ ῥήματα ποικίλως ἐξητάσαμεν· νῦν δ᾿ αὐτὰ εἰς τὸ προκείμενον ἁπλούστερον κατὰ τὴν κοινοτέραν ἐκδοχὴν παρειλήφαμεν, ἐπείπερ φησὶν ὁ Κέλσος· οὐδὲ τούτους ἄνευ δαιμονίας ἰσχύος τῶν τῇδε εἶναι ἠξιωμένους. καὶ ἐπεὶ πολὺς ἦν ὁ λόγος ὁ περὶ τῆς τῶν βασιλευόντων καὶ δυναστῶν καταστάσεως, πολλῆς ζητήσεως οὔσης κατὰ τὸν τόπον διὰ τοὺς ὠμότερον καὶ τυραννικώτερον ἄρξαντας ἢ τοὺς ἐκ τοῦ ἄρχειν ἐπὶ θρύψιν καὶ τρυφὴν ἐξοκείλαντας, διὰ τοῦτο ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος τὸ πρόβλημα ἐξετάσαι ὑπερεθέμεθα. τύχην μέντοι βασιλέως οὐκ ὄμνυμεν ὡς οὐδ᾿ ἄλλον νομιζόμενον θεόν· εἴτε γὰρ, ὡς ὠνόμασάν τινες, ἐκφορὰ μόνον ἐστὶν ἡ τύχη ὁμοίως δοκήσει καὶ διαστάσει, οὐκ ὄμνυμεν τὸ μηδαμῶς ὂν ὡς θεὸν ἢ ὅλως ὑφεστηκὸς καὶ δυνάμενόν τι ποιῆσαι, ἵνα μὴ τὴν ὀμοτικὴν δύναμιν εἰς ἃ μὴ δεῖ παραλαμβάνωμεν, εἴτε καὶ (ὥς τισιν ἔδοξεν εἰποῦσι· τοῦ Ῥωμαίων βασιλέως τὸν δαίμονα ὀμνῦσιν οἱ τὴν τύχην αὐτοῦ ὀμνύοντες) δαίμων ἐστὶν ἡ ὀνομαζομένη τύχη τοῦ βασιλέως, καὶ οὕτως ἀποθανετέον ἐστὶ μᾶλλον ἡμῖν ὑπὲρ τοῦ μὴ ὀμόσαι μοχθηρὸν δαίμονα καὶ ἄπιστον, πολλάκις συνεξαμαρτάνοντα ᾧ ἔλαχεν ἀνθρώπῳ ἢ καὶ πλέον αὐτοῦ ἁμαρτάνοντα.
pass_a_gloss: By us, however, the winning-of-favour (ἐξευμενισμός) of men and kings must be despised (καταφρονητέον), not only if through murders (μιαιφονία) and licentiousness (ἀσέλγεια) and most savage (ὠμότατος) deeds we would propitiate (ἐξευμενίζω) them, but also if through impiety (ἀσέβεια) toward the God of the universe (θεὸς τῶν ὅλων) or some utterance (φωνή) with servility (δουλοπρέπεια) and abjectness (ταπεινότης), foreign (ἀλλότριος) to brave (ἀνδρεῖος) and great-souled (μεγαλόψυχος) men who wish to take up together (συναναλαμβάνω) endurance (καρτερία) as greatest virtue (ἀρετή) with the others. Where, however, we do nothing contrary to the law (νόμος) and word/Word (λόγος) of God, we are not mad (μαίνομαι, perfect μεμήναμεν), nor do we rush (ὁρμάω) to rouse (ἐγείρω) against ourselves the anger (θυμός) of a king or ruler (δυνάστης), bringing us to outrages (αἰκία) and tortures (βασανιστήριον) or even deaths. For we have read also: 'Let every soul be subject (ὑποτάσσω) to authorities (ἐξουσία) that are over (ὑπερέχω). For there is no authority except under/from God, and those that are have been ordered (τάσσω) by God; so that those who resist (ἀνθίστημι) the authority resist the ordinance (διαταγή) of God.' In our exegetical works (ἐξηγητικά) on the Epistle to the Romans, as was possible for us, we examined (ἐξετάζω) these words more fully and variously (ποικίλως); but now we have taken (παραλαμβάνω) them for the matter at hand (τὸ προκείμενον) more simply (ἁπλούστερον) according to the more common interpretation (κοινοτέρα ἐκδοχή), since Celsus says: 'Not even these (men) have been deemed worthy (ἀξιόω) of the things here (τὰ τῇδε) without demonic power (δαιμονία ἰσχύς).' And since the discussion (λόγος) about the appointment/establishment (κατάστασις) of those who reign and rulers was large, there being much inquiry (ζήτησις) on the passage (τόπος) because of those who ruled more cruelly (ὠμότερον) and more tyrannically (τυραννικώτερον), or those who from ruling ran aground (ἐξοκέλλω) into softness (θρύψις) and luxury (τρυφή), for this reason we postponed (ὑπερτίθημι) examining the problem (πρόβλημα) for the present. We do not, however, swear (ὄμνυμι) by the fortune (τύχη) of the king/emperor, as neither by another supposed (νομιζόμενος) god; for whether, as some have named it, fortune is only an expression/manner of speaking (ἐκφορά), like 'seeming' (δόκησις) and 'distance/extension' (διάστασις), we do not swear by what in no way is (τὸ μηδαμῶς ὄν) as a god, or as altogether subsisting (ὑφεστηκός) and able to do something, so that we may not apply (παραλαμβάνω) the oath-power (ὀμοτικὴ δύναμις) to what we should not; or whether (as it seemed to some who said: 'those swearing by his fortune swear by the daemon of the Roman king') the so-called fortune of the king is a daemon (δαίμων), and so we must die (ἀποθανετέον) rather for the sake of not swearing by a wicked (μοχθηρός) and faithless (ἄπιστος) daemon, often sinning together with (συνεξαμαρτάνω) the man to whom it was allotted (λαγχάνω), or even sinning more than he.
pass_b_english: We, however, must scorn to win the favour of men and kings, not only if we would win it by murders, by debauchery and by the most savage deeds, but also if we would win it by impiety toward the God of the universe, or by any word spoken with servility and abjectness. Such words are foreign to brave and great-souled men, who wish to take up endurance, as the greatest of virtues, together with the other virtues. Yet where we do nothing contrary to the law and word of God, we are not mad, nor are we eager to rouse against ourselves the anger of a king or a ruler, which would bring us to outrages and tortures, or even to death. For we have also read: “Let every soul be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been appointed by God; so whoever resists the authority resists what God has ordained” (Romans 13:1–2).

In our commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans we examined these words too, more fully and from various sides, as far as we were able. Here we have taken them more simply, according to the more common interpretation, to suit the matter in hand, since Celsus says: “Not even these men have been granted the things of this world without the power of demons.” And since the subject of the appointment of kings and rulers is a large one, and the passage raises much inquiry because of those who have ruled with cruelty and tyranny, or those who, once in power, have run aground on softness and luxury, we have for that reason put off examining the problem for the present.

We do not, however, swear by the fortune of the emperor, any more than by any other supposed god. For if, as some have put it, fortune is only a way of speaking, like “seeming” and “distance,” then we do not swear by what does not exist at all as though it were a god, or as though it had any real existence and could do anything, so that we may not apply the power of an oath where it ought not to be applied. Or if, as some have held when they say, “Those who swear by the fortune of the Roman emperor swear by his demon,” what is called the emperor’s fortune is a demon, then in that case we must rather die than swear by a wicked and faithless demon, which often sins along with the man to whom it was allotted, or even sins more than he does.

choices.choice: βασιλεύς is rendered ‘king’ in the general statements and ‘emperor’ where the Roman emperor’s fortune (the oath by the emperor’s genius/tyche) is meant; the Greek uses one word. The Romans quotation follows Origen’s wording (ἐξουσίαις ὑπερεχούσαις; εἰ μὴ ὑπὸ θεοῦ; οἱ ἀνθεστηκότες), close to the received text of Romans 13:1-2. Celsus’s sentence (‘Not even these men...’) is quoted from the preceding argument (compare 8.63); its referent is rulers and kings. ‘ἐκφορὰ μόνον ... ὁμοίως δοκήσει καὶ διαστάσει’: a philosophical (probably Stoic) view that ‘fortune’ is a mere word with no subsistent reality, like ‘seeming’ and ‘distance’; the exact sense of δόκησις and διάστασις here is uncertain, and they are rendered literally. The commentary on Romans referred to is Origen’s own (largely surviving in Rufinus’s Latin). The emperor’s ‘demon’ renders δαίμων as elsewhere in this translation (house usage: demon). ‘the law and word of God’ (νόμῳ καὶ λόγῳ θεοῦ) is lowercased: here God’s revealed teaching, not the person of the Word. ‘scorn to win the favour’ renders καταφρονητέον ἐξευμενισμοῦ (literally ‘the propitiating ... must be despised’).
'must think nothing of winning the favour' -> 'must scorn to win the favour' (καταφρονητέον = despise; old wording could read as 'do it easily')
'law and Word of God' -> 'law and word of God' (λόγος here = God's teaching, not the Logos)
'together with the rest' -> 'together with the other virtues' (ταῖς ἄλλαις = virtues)
'let their rule carry them aground' -> 'who, once in power, have run aground' (agency stays with the rulers, ἐξοκείλαντας)
'for we would not apply' -> 'so that we may not apply' (ἵνα μή is purpose)
'as some have thought, saying' -> 'as some have held when they say'; 'in this case too we ought rather' -> 'in that case we must rather' (ἀποθανετέον)
Romans 13:1-2 checked against the Greek: correct
